items.title: Hindu deities are often understood as manifestations of one Brahman
items.claim: How does Hindu theology relate the many gods to Brahman?

options.text: Each god is wholly separate and independent

Many Hindus understand the gods as manifestations (devas) of one ultimate reality (Brahman) — though the relationship varies between traditions; the Rig Veda (1.164.46) says 'Truth is one; sages call it by many names'
There is only one god — Brahma alone

items.reveal:
The Trimurti (Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer) is one classical mapping of cosmic functions.

Vaishnavism centres on Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna). Shaivism centres on Shiva. Shaktism centres on Devi/Shakti (the divine feminine — Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati). Each tradition may treat its chosen deity as supreme.

The term 'henotheism' (worshipping one god while acknowledging others) was coined by Max Müller in the 19th century specifically to describe Vedic religion.
items.why: Calling Hinduism polytheistic or monotheistic both miss the structure. The 'many manifestations of one' framework is philosophically distinct — and shapes how Hindus actually relate to images and shrines.

items.title: Shabbat begins on Friday evening, not Saturday
items.claim: When does the Jewish Sabbath begin and end?

options.text: It runs from Saturday morning to Sunday morning
From sunset on Friday to the appearance of three stars on Saturday night — Jewish days begin at sunset, following Genesis 1's 'and there was evening and there was morning'
It is calculated by the Gregorian clock

items.reveal:
The Genesis creation account marks each day 'there was evening and there was morning' — establishing the Jewish day as evening to evening. Shabbat is welcomed with candle lighting (typically 18 minutes before sunset) and Kiddush over wine.

The Torah commands rest from melacha — 39 categories of work derived from the activities involved in building the Tabernacle. These include lighting fires, writing, carrying in public, tearing, cooking. Modern applications (electricity, driving, mobile phones) follow rabbinic reasoning by analogy.

Shabbat ends with Havdalah — a brief ceremony with wine, spices and a multi-wick candle separating the holy from the ordinary.
items.why: Religious time is structured differently. Treating Shabbat as 'Saturday' misses both its beginning at sunset and the depth of its observance — which is one of the most distinctive elements of Jewish practice.

items.title: Every Sikh gurdwara serves langar — a free meal for all

options.text: A meal sold to support the gurdwara

A free communal meal served to anyone regardless of religion, caste, gender or background — a foundational Sikh practice originated by Guru Nanak and institutionalised by Guru Amar Das (3rd Guru), who required visitors to eat langar before meeting him

items.reveal:
Langar is served in the langar hall of every gurdwara worldwide. All sit on the floor at the same level — explicitly rejecting caste hierarchy. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar) serves around 100,000 meals daily; volunteers prepare and clean.

Guru Amar Das (1479-1574) made eating langar a requirement before meeting him — including for the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who reportedly sat with peasants before being granted an audience.

In the UK, Sikh organisations like Khalsa Aid extend the langar tradition to refugees, food banks and disaster response — in Ukraine, Turkey after the 2023 earthquake, and at UK floods.
items.why: Practice can teach doctrine. Sitting on the floor and eating together puts equality into the body — more direct than verbal teaching.
